title: Averages, Medians, and Data Traps
description: Practice identifying when common statistical measures mislead and how to choose the right metric for business decisions.

interactions.prompt: A SaaS startup reports: mean customer spend is $450/mo, median is $85/mo, and the top 2% of accounts spend over $8,000/mo. What's the key insight?

options.text: Most customers spend around $450/mo
The distribution is heavily right-skewed by whale accounts
The median is unreliable due to small sample size
Revenue is evenly distributed across customer segments

interactions.prompt: When a dataset has extreme outliers, the ____ is a more reliable measure of central tendency than the mean because it resists distortion from extreme values.

options.text: Standard deviation
Median
Mode
Variance

interactions.prompt: Spotify's data team finds that users who create playlists have 3x higher retention. A PM proposes auto-creating playlists for new users to boost retention. What's the flaw?

options.text: The sample size is probably too small to draw conclusions
Playlist creation likely signals engagement, not causes it
3x is not a statistically significant difference
Retention should be measured over a longer time period

chartData.title: User Retention Rate by Playlist Creation Behavior

interactions.prompt: You're launching a pricing experiment at Shopify. You can test with 200 merchants over 8 weeks for directional data, or 2,000 merchants over 3 weeks for statistical significance. Budget allows only one. Which do you choose?

options.text: 200 merchants, 8 weeks — captures seasonal behavior patterns
2,000 merchants, 3 weeks — larger sample yields more reliable results
Split the budget and run both simultaneously at half scale
Skip the experiment and use historical pricing data instead

interactions.prompt: Netflix sees that a new recommendation algorithm increases watch time by 6% in a 5,000-user test (p=0.04), but qualitative feedback from 30 users says suggestions feel "creepy." How do you proceed?

options.text: Ship it — statistically significant lift in the core metric wins
Run a larger qualitative study before deciding on rollout
Ignore qualitative data — 30 users is too small to matter
Roll out to 50% of users and monitor churn for tradeoffs

interactions.prompt: Rank these red flags from MOST to LEAST concerning when reviewing a competitor's published market research claiming their product leads the category:

options.text: Survey sample of only 50 respondents nationwide
No confidence intervals or margin of error reported
Results rounded to nearest whole percentage
Respondents were recruited from the company's own customer base

interactions.prompt: Your e-commerce team sees average order value (AOV) jumped 22% last month. Rank these diagnostic steps from FIRST to LAST to understand what happened:

options.text: Check if a few large B2B orders are skewing the mean
Compare median order value to see if typical customers changed
Celebrate the win and set higher AOV targets for next quarter
Segment by channel to see if the lift is broad or isolated

interactions.prompt: You now learn that 40% of the 2,000-merchant sample in your Shopify pricing test were enterprise accounts, while enterprise is only 8% of your actual merchant base. How does this change your conclusion?

options.text: Results are still valid — 2,000 is a large enough sample
Results are biased — the sample doesn't represent your population
Only use data from the enterprise segment going forward
Double the sample size to compensate for the skew

interactions.priorContext: Earlier you chose to run a 2,000-merchant pricing test at Shopify for statistical significance. You assumed the sample was representative of your merchant base.
